claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure.
The hierarchical heterostructure is retained under standard solution-treatment and quenching conditions.
In-situ tensile and fracture measurements can capture near-crack-tip microstructural and crack-propagation events.
Real-time in-situ data can be used to calibrate a cohesive-zone model for HfNbTiVAl10.
A cohesive-zone finite-element framework can be informed directly by imaging crack initiation and propagation at critical heterophase interfaces.
Local damage and plasticity information from in-situ testing constrains cohesive traction laws.
The calibrated cohesive-zone model captures the multiscale mechanical response of the alloy's hierarchical interfaces.
In-situ-informed cohesive modeling reduces the need for ab initio or fully meshed finite-element fracture simulations.
Ab initio and related high-fidelity computational approaches can be too time-consuming or resource-intensive for high-throughput alloy discovery.
CALPHAD can require significant computing resources and can be limited by the availability of reliable high-entropy-alloy databases.
Machine-learning methods have previously been used to predict alloy yield strength, Young's modulus, and toughness-related properties.
The proposed method will reduce total computational cost by at least 50%.
The proposed method will improve prediction accuracy for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness by 30% relative to HPC-based or first-principles methods.
The method is applicable at ambient to moderate temperatures when the hierarchical heterostructure remains consistent with the calibrated microstructure.
Unforeseen phase transformations or partitioning into additional phases can invalidate the calibrated model.
Extreme temperatures, extended service times, or non-standard processing routes may cause the method to cease being reliable.
Irregular interface morphology or incomplete crack-path control could reduce predictive fidelity below the anticipated 30% improvement.
Prior integrations of in-situ data and cohesive modeling indicate the feasibility of the proposed approach.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis limits the expected accuracy improvement to 'up to 30%,' whereas the predicted outcome states a 30% improvement without qualification; these imply different performance bounds.
The hypothesis describes computational-overhead reduction as 'about half,' while the predicted outcome requires 'at least 50%,' changing an approximate estimate into a lower-bound guarantee.
